<div class="course-section-head" id="course-curiosities"><h2>Explore further</h2></div>

<div class="course-curiosities">
<details>
<summary>Moving a figure does not replace a proof</summary>

Changing a construction can show that a property persists. This helps form a conjecture, but a proof must explain why it holds for **every** figure satisfying the hypotheses.

Try moving the congruence controls and identify which data remain equal.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="congruency-chapter-1.html#geometry-fig-3">Explore congruence →</a></p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>An angle that stays constant</summary>

An inscribed angle measures half its intercepted arc. If its vertex moves along the same arc while the chord endpoints stay fixed, the angle stays constant.

Explore what happens on the other arc: identify the arc that **does not contain** the vertex.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="congruency-chapter-1.html#geometry-fig-7">Explore the inscribed-angle theorem →</a></p>
</details>

<details>
<summary>Three projections, one line</summary>

Simson’s theorem states that the perpendicular projections of a point on a triangle’s circumcircle onto the three side lines are collinear.

Move the point and observe that the feet can lie beyond the side segments while remaining aligned.

<p class="curiosity-link"><a href="congruency-chapter-1.html#geometry-fig-12">Explore the Simson line →</a></p>
</details>

</div>
